newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - European woes to weigh heavily.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - European woes to weigh heavily.

text.p: UK gilts are expected to struggle to escape the gloom surrounding European bonds this week but domestic events should be supportive, with Wednesday's auction set to go well and retail sales expected to show slower consumer spending.
"We don't have a huge amount to focus on this week but what news we get on the economy should be healthy," said Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW.
"Retail sales should show a slowdown and the CBI monthly survey on Wednesday will hopefully show export orders have bounced, making industry less vulnerable to a rate rise after the election."
None of the domestic data is due until Wednesday, however, leaving gilts at the mercy of panic-struck Europe in the meantime.

European bonds and shares sank in early Monday trade as investors grew unsettled by the prospect of a snap French election, the result of which could determine the outlook for European monetary union.
Worries seeped into gilts and futures, which were marked down at the open. The June futures contract opened at 109-16, down 8/32 from Friday close.
But traders said a wages survey out over the weekend was proving supportive and set the stage for gilts to outperform beleagured Bunds, if only modestly.

The Confederation of British Industry reported pay settlements were very subdued in both services and manufacturing industries -- up 3.7 and 3.2 percent respectively in the first quarter -- helping to offset fears wage growth is too strong.
The yield spread to Bunds narrowed slightly to 184 basis points in early trade from 185 on Friday.

Retail sales data provide the week's first concrete domestic focus. The Reuter consensus forecast suggests retail sales rose 0.3 percent in March, allowing the year-on-year growth rate to slow to 4.3 percent from 4.4 percent in February.

"Any evidence that there are resisting forces at work in the economy will be greeted with delight by gilts," said a senior trader at a U.S. bank. "It means any monetary tightening needn't be as drastic as short sterling is discounting."
The short sterling strip is discounting a half point rate rise by the end of June and another half point by the year-end.
A soft retail sales number would put the market on a more certain footing for the auction of 2.0 billion stg of 7.0 percent gilts due 2002 on Wednesday.

"These short maturity gilts have cheapened up recently and with only 2.0 billion stg for sale the auction should not be a problem," said Joanne Collins, bond analyst at Nomura. However, overseas investors may be cautious with the May 1 election looming, she added.

Adams at BZW said the auction stock has long been trading at a special rate in the repo market, which suggests plenty of pent up demand. "Much of the stock seems to be in the hands of overseas investors who are not lending it out, so there should be good demand on Wednesday."

Later in the week, the British Chambers of Commerce first quarter survey on Thursday and official GDP data on Friday should provide direction. Both are expected to show service industry growth continued unabated in the period.

The Reuters poll forecasts GDP grew 0.9 percent in the first quarter, pushing the year-on year growth rate up to 2.9 percent compared with 2.6 percent in the last quarter of 1996. Analysts said they did not expect any dramatic movements in the yield curve this week, nor until the aftermath of the election when interest rates are set to rise whoever wins.

"The short end may be vulnerable during the period after the election and before a rate rise which may stretch out until June. I can't see a new Chancellor raising rates just days after he takes office," said Adams.

If the opinion polls are right, opposition Labour's finance spokesman Gordon Brown will become the next Chancellor of the Exchequer. The first monetary meeting is scheduled for May 7, less than a week after he would take office. Adams forecasts the two-to-10-year spread will narrow to around 50 basis point after the first rate rise taken place from 65 basis point at present.
